entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The phrase "There once was a man" can begin a parable (symbolic story with asocial meanings) or a historical account (2 Samuel 12:1; 1 Samuel 25:2).

• Ezekiel 14:14, Ezekiel 14:20 and James 5:11 also mention Job.

• Uz is east of the Jordan River, either in Edom to the south or in Aram to the north (Genesis 36:28; 1 Chronicles 1:42; Jeremiah 25:19–20; Lamentations 4:21; Genesis 10:23; Genesis 22:21; 1 Chronicles 1:17, 1 Chronicles 1:42). Job was not from Israel. He lived before the nation of Israel existed and outside its later territory.

• Job had no moral faults, he was a man of complete integrity (Job 1:8; Job 2:3; see Psalms 25:21; Psalms 37:37; Proverbs 2:7; Proverbs 20:11; Proverbs 29:10). He did not claim to be perfect or without sin (Job 6:24; Job 7:21; see also Ecclesiastes 7:20; Romans 3:23; 1 John 1:8). But he was righteous (in a right relationship with God) so his suffering was not because of guilt. Here, fearing God probably means he did not worship any Ancient Near Eastern gods (see Psalms 111:10; Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10; 2 Corinthians 7:1; Job 9:8; Job 23:13; Job 31:26–28).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: God and Satan agree to test Job, which causes his troubles and confirms his integrity (Job 1:20–21; Job 2:10). None of the book's characters ever learn of this council in heaven.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• God gave Job prosperity with many sons, daughters, cattle and other domestic animals, and servants (compare Genesis 30:43; Deuteronomy 7:13; Psalm 107:38).

• Numbers like seven and three (and 7,000 and 3,000) show the full extent of God's blessings for Job (see Job 42:13; also see Psalms 127:3–5; Psalms 128:3).

• Job was the greatest man of all the people of the East: The numbers describing Job’s wealth might not be exact, but they are realistic for a wealthy man of that time (compare Nabal’s wealth in 1 Samuel 25:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• People often washed and changed clothes to purify themselves before making a sacrifice (Genesis 35:2; Exodus 19:10, Exodus 19:14).

• The usual time for sincere religious dedication was early morning (see Genesis 22:3; Psalm 5:3; Mark 1:35). 

• cursed: The Hebrew verb barak (usually meaning blessed) used here is a polite way to say "cursed" (compare Job 1:11; Job 2:5, Job 2:9; 1 Kings 21:10, 1 Kings 21:13; Psalm 10:3). Job worried that his children might have committed this serious crime (Leviticus 24:10–16; 1 Kings 21:9–13; compare Job 1:11; Job 2:5, Job 2:9). Job knew that God regards wrong attitudes as sin (Jeremiah 17:9–10; Mark 7:21–23).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• These sons of God are spiritual beings and members of the court of heaven. They are probably either holy angels or demons (Genesis 6:2, Genesis 6:4). They join God in his discussions, including during creation and in his rule over creation (Genesis 1:26; Job 1:6; Genesis 3:22; Genesis 2:1; 1 Kings 22:19–22; Psalms 82:1; Psalms 89:5, Psalms 89:7–8; Daniel 3:13, Daniel 3:17, Daniel 3:23, Daniel 3:25; Daniel 7:9–14).

• It is uncertain in the account if Satan usually came with other court members of heaven to report or if he forced his way in as Job’s opponent.

• "Where have you come from?": This question was God’s command for a report from one of his subjects (see Genesis 3:9).

• Satan was not roaming through the earth to do God’s will (compare 1 Chronicles 21:1–14; 2 Kings 19:35 is equivalent to Isaiah 37:36; Ezekiel 1:5–9). Instead, he opposes God’s plans (2 Timothy 2:26; 1 Peter 5:8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
My servant: 

People used this title for:

• The patriarchs ("first fathers") of Israel (Genesis 26:24; Exodus 32:13).

• The prophets (2 Kings 17:13; Jeremiah 7:25; Zechariah 1:6).

• King David (for example, 2 Samuel 7:1–29; Psalms 18:1; Psalms 36:1).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job has a good reason (Hebrew khinnam; see study note on 2:3) to fear God. The wisdom tradition connects being religious with prosperity. Satan suggested that Job's dedication to God depended on his wealth.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: a hedge on every side: See 1 Samuel 25:16; Psalms 5:12; Psalms 34:7; Zechariah 2:5; compare Isaiah 5:5.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Stretch out … and strike all he has … Everything he has is in your hands: Satan was God's agent. The hand he used was both the Lord's and Satan's. They acted against everything Job owned and later against Job himself (Job 2:5–6).

• Job later cursed the day of his birth, but he did not curse God (Job 3:1, Job 3:8; Job 31:30). This was even true when his upset wife urged him to do so (Job 2:9).

• God allowed Satan to test Job to show that Satan's negative view of Job was wrong (1 Corinthians 10:11; see James 1:13; compare Luke 22:31–32; John 19:11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• These attacks took away the blessings listed in Job 1:2–3. Job was left with four messengers who came to report terrible news and a wife who gave poor advice.

• The phrase "While he was still speaking" emphasizes the repeated nature of the attacks (see Jeremiah 51:31). The phrase "I alone have escaped to tell you" emphasizes the complete destruction of Job’s resources.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The Sabeans were tribes who raided from the desert (compare Judges 6:3). By the 700s BC, the southern Sabeans became a powerful nation. They traded in gold, precious stones, sweet smelling liquids, and slaves (see Psalm 72:10; Isaiah 43:3; Isaiah 45:14; Isaiah 60:6; Jeremiah 6:20).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The fire of God … from heaven: This might have been lightning, fire in the desert, or the activity of a volcano (Job 20:26; Leviticus 10:2; 1 Kings 18:38; 2 Kings 1:10–14; Numbers 11:1–3; Genesis 19:24).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: a mighty wind …struck the four corners of the house: This suggests that Job and his children were farmers settled and living in houses, not people wandering about and living in tents (nomads).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Job stood up, tore his robe, and shaved his head: These were common ceremonies in the Ancient Near East to show grief. People sometimes responded this way instead of harming themselves when shocked, in horror, or after hearing bad news (Job 2:12; Genesis 37:29, Genesis 37:34; Judges 11:35; Jeremiah 16:6; Ezekiel 7:18; Amos 8:10).

• He fell to the ground and worshiped: Then in an unexpected move, Job did not give a desperate cry, but had hope (1 Peter 5:6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: This scene repeats exactly as it did in Job 1:6–8.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The phrase without cause (Hebrew khinnam) is a play on words from Satan's question in Job 1:9.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: strike his flesh and bones: People once believed bones were the source of health.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: spare (literally guard or watch over): Ironically, God made Satan responsible for guarding Job’s life (compare Job 10:13–14; Job 13:27; Job 33:11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: This Hebrew term for terrible boils referred to any raised wounds that leak (Exodus 9:10; Leviticus 13:18–20; Deuteronomy 28:27, Deuteronomy 28:35).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Job might have scraped his skin for relief. The ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) says it was “to scrape away the pus.” 

• The ashes might refer to a place where they placed lepers in isolation. But Job was probably showing his grief and how desperate he was (Job 30:19; Genesis 18:27; 2 Samuel 13:19; Isaiah 58:5; Jonah 3:6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's wife first summarized Job's temptation by echoing God's words. Job was trying to "retain his integrity" (Job 2:3). In her frustration and pain, she then advised Job to curse God. Without knowing it, she was asking Job to fulfill Satan's prediction (Job 1:11; Job 2:5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Job accepted both good and bad things from God, showing his right relationship and faith in God (righteousness) (compare Job 1:21; 2 Samuel 12:16–20; Luke 22:42).

• By saying nothing wrong, Job controlled his tongue (Proverbs 13:3; Proverbs 21:23; see James 3:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• It might have taken several months for Job’s three friends to learn about his troubles (see study note on 6:14–27; see Job 7:3). 

• The text suggests that Job’s three friends were Edomites, a people known for their wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 1:8). 

• Eliphaz the Temanite was probably a descendant of Esau’s grandson Teman (Genesis 36:10–11, Genesis 36:15). His land was in Edom (Ezekiel 25:13; Amos 1:11–12). 

• The "Bil-" part of the name "Bildad" would remind Hebrew readers of names like Bilhan, a descendant of Esau (Genesis 36:27; 1 Chronicles 1:42). The "-dad" part of the name would remind readers of names like Bedad, father of the Edomite king Hadad (Genesis 36:35; 1 Chronicles 1:46). 

• Shuhite: No place named "Shuah" is known, but Abraham’s son "Shuah" was sent to “a land in the east” (Genesis 25:1, Genesis 25:6; 1 Chronicles 1:32).

• The ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) lists Zophar instead of "Zepho" as one of Esau’s grandsons (Genesis 36:11, Genesis 36:15; 1 Chronicles 1:36). A Naamathite might live in a town named "Naamah." But no such place is known. Two Old Testament women are named "Naamah," but neither is likely an ancestor of Zophar (Genesis 4:22; 1 Kings 14:21).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• They could barely recognize Job: This expression shows how much Job had suffered (compare Isaiah 52:14; Isaiah 53:3). 

• Job’s friends showed their grief and began to weep aloud, as if Job was dead. 

• Throwing dust sometimes showed anger or hate (see 2 Samuel 16:13; Acts 22:23). But here it showed grief (see Joshua 7:6; 1 Samuel 4:12; Nehemiah 9:1; Lamentations 2:10).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Job’s friends sat on the ground to share in Job’s suffering (see Job 2:8).

• People usually showed grief for seven days and nights when an important person died or to acknowledge other bad news (Genesis 50:10; 1 Samuel 31:13; see also Ezekiel 3:14–15).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Job spoke and risked words of sin (Job 1:21; Job 2:10).

• Job cursed the day of his birth in great detail. However, his words sounded more like sad complaints. Job did not curse God as his creator, but he showed grief about the condition of his life.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's outbreak of emotion did not mean his integrity failed under pressure (Job 42:7–8; James 5:11). The prophets Elijah and Jeremiah, both men of God, exaggerated with similar language (1 Kings 19:4; Jeremiah 20:14–18).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job wished that the darkness of the place of the dead and the gloom of death had not allowed him to be born (Exodus 10:22; Proverbs 4:19; Joel 2:2; Job 10:21–22; Job 38:17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The phrase those who curse the day refers to people paid to curse, like Balaam (Numbers 22–24).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Venus and Mercury, known as the morning stars, announce the arrival of dawn (Job 38:7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: shut the doors of the womb: Closing or opening the womb can mean conception (Genesis 16:2; Genesis 20:18; Genesis 29:31; Genesis 30:22; 1 Samuel 1:5–6). But here it means birth (see also Job 38:8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's language shifts from wishing he was never born to grief. He goes from hating life towards an attraction for death. Job asks "why" seven times, as he has grief for his situation (Job 3:11, Job 3:12, Job 3:16, Job 3:20, Job 3:23; see Psalms 10:1; Psalms 22:1; Jeremiah 20:18; Lamentations 5:20).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: People believed the dead kept their identities and social status. Job might have wanted kings and prime ministers to recognize his status as a prince (Job 1:3).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: who had gold, who filled their houses with silver: This might refer to tombs filled with treasure. However, it more likely refers to the useless storing of wealth that ends in death (as in Job 3:14).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Job compared light to life (Job 33:30; see John 1:4; John 8:12).

• Bitter might mean:

• “Angry” (Judges 18:25).

• “Fierce” (2 Samuel 17:8).

• “Anguish” (Job 7:11).

• Desperate (Proverbs 31:6).

• “Distress” (1 Samuel 1:10; 1 Samuel 22:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: People in grief desperately long for death, like those who search for hidden treasure.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Eliphaz the Temanite was probably the oldest and most important of Job’s friends (see study note on 2:11). His speeches are longer and more detailed than the others.

• who can keep from speaking?: Eliphaz imitated how urgent a message from prophets can be (Job 4:12–16; see Jeremiah 20:9; Amos 3:8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: This section starts three rounds of speeches by Job's three "comforters," each followed by Job's response (Job 4:1–27:23). In the first round, Job's friends urge him to seek God to regain prosperity.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: These were people who were weak, felt depressed, and had low confidence in themselves (Isaiah 13:7; Isaiah 35:3; Ezekiel 7:17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job probably considered his children among the innocent who died (Job 1:5). Even Eliphaz must have known that people sometimes "shed innocent blood" (compare Deuteronomy 19:10; Proverbs 6:17; Jeremiah 7:6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The symbolic use of the language of harvest shows the idea in the Scriptures that actions deserve judgment (Proverbs 22:8; Hosea 8:7; Romans 2:9–11; Galatians 6:7–8). The New Testament compares the final judgment to a harvest (Matthew 13:39). By this principle, Jesus rejected overly simple attempts to analyze people's lives (Luke 13:4; John 9:1–3).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: by the blast of His anger they are consumed: Eliphaz saw the wind in Job 1:19 as God's judgment (compare Isaiah 40:7; Hosea 13:15).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Eliphaz claimed to be a prophet, suggesting that God spoke to him secretly (Numbers 12:6). Later, God did speak to him, but not to support his advice (Job 42:7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Eliphaz probably referred to the sleep caused by God that links to the visions given to prophets (Job 33:15; Genesis 15:12; Numbers 12:6; Isaiah 29:10).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Fear often occurs in God's presence (Genesis 15:12; Daniel 8:17–18; Daniel 10:8–10). But God tells his people not to fear (Genesis 15:1; Genesis 26:24; Isaiah 40:9; Isaiah 44:8).

• Eliphaz's bones shook like those of a prophet with terrible news to share (Jeremiah 23:9; Habakkuk 3:16).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: a spirit (or wind) glided past my face: Wind shows God's powerful presence in a physical way (Job 38:1; Nahum 1:3; Acts 2:2; compare 1 Kings 19:11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The characters in the book often say that no one is truly righteous or pure (see Job 9:2; Job 15:14; Job 25:4; Job 35:7). This is because everyone is flawed (Psalms 14:3; Psalms 53:3; Romans 3:10–11). Eliphaz used these terms to say that humans are full of sin and God has no sin. Job and God used them to show that Job had fulfilled his duties to God. Job and Eliphaz never agreed on what these terms meant. Later, God said that Eliphaz had not spoken about him "accurately" (Job 42:7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The idea that God does not trust His servants and charges His angels with error is unique (but see Genesis 6:1–4).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: A tent often symbolized human life (Isaiah 38:12; 2 Corinthians 5:1; compare Ecclesiastes 12:6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The holy ones probably refers back to the angels mentioned in Job 4:18. They are "holy ones" because of they are close to God, not because they have achieved moral perfection (Job 15:15; Daniel 4:14; Daniel 8:13; Zechariah 14:5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: in court: Literally this reads, in the gate. At that time, legal and business discussions happened. Job participated in these discussions (Job 29:7; see Deuteronomy 21:19–21; Ruth 4:1–11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Appeal to God: This meant a formal request for help, advice, or removal of blame, sometimes through asking God to forgive (Amos 5:4, Amos 5:6). It could possibly refer to an appeal through a message from a prophet (Genesis 25:22; 1 Samuel 9:9; 1 Kings 22:8).

• Job wanted to present his cause before God. Later he tried to do that very thing (Job 13:3, Job 13:15, Job 13:18; Job 23:3–8; Job 29:1–31:40).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The region where Job lived relied on rain instead of human methods to water crops (see Job 36:27–28).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Eliphaz praised God as the creator and and the one who sustains the universe who performs wonders (Job 5:9–10). He also praised God as the righteous judge who humbles the powerful and honors poor people (Job 5:11–16).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: God catches the wise in their craftiness (Proverbs 12:13). The apostle Paul referred to this idea when he rejected the wisdom of the world (1 Corinthians 1:19).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: the discipline of the Almighty: See Deuteronomy 8:5; Proverbs 3:11–12; Revelation 3:19.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Six calamities … in seven: This formula for wise sayings suggests a condition of completion (compare Proverbs 30:15–31).

• This list reflects the blessings and curses of the covenant God gave to Moses (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28). 

Eliphaz believed that people in a right relationship with God would avoid: 

• Famine, meaning starving. (Job 5:20, Job 5:22; see Leviticus 26:4–5, Leviticus 26:10; Deuteronomy 28:4–6, Deuteronomy 28:8, Deuteronomy 28:11–12).

• Battle and its destruction (Job 5:20; Job 5:21, Job 5:22; see Leviticus 26:6–8; Deuteronomy 28:7, Deuteronomy 28:48).

• Scourge of the tongue, or words spoken against them (slander).

• They would even be at peace with wild animals and the stones of the field (Job 5:23; see Leviticus 26:6). This peace might mean productive fields instead of rocky ones (2 Kings 3:19, 2 Kings 3:25; Matthew 13:5). Or it might symbolize broader harmony with creation (see Psalm 91:11–12).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: nothing amiss: See Deuteronomy 28:11–12; compare with Job 1:6–19.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: descendants like the grass of the earth: See Genesis 22:17; Leviticus 26:9; Deuteronomy 28:4, Deuteronomy 28:11–12.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job responds by criticizing his counselors and questioning God (chapters Job 6:6 and Job 7:7). He explains his intense words by indicating his deep "grief" or "anguish" (Job 6:2–3; Job 7:11). Job states that Eliphaz has not provided comfort or sympathy as a friend. Instead, Eliphaz chose to argue about out of date religious or theological ideas.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: In the Old Testament, arrows symbolize danger, disease, and destruction from God (Job 7:20; Job 16:12–13; Deuteronomy 32:23–24, Deuteronomy 32:42; Psalms 7:12–13; Psalms 38:2; Psalms 64:7; Psalms 91:5–6; Lamentations 2:4; Lamentations 3:12–13; Ezekiel 5:16).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The tasteless food … the white of an egg? Job's complaint in the form of a word puzzle (riddle) probably refers to both Eliphaz's weak advice and the situation God allowed him to endure that Job hates.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: At one time, both the prophets Moses and Elijah asked God to end their lives (Numbers 11:15; 1 Kings 19:4).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job and his friends might have shared a covenant (special agreement) of loyalty and faith (Hebrew khesed; see Genesis 21:23; Exodus 15:13; 1 Chronicles 16:34). This bond would have made them like brothers, those who protect, and friends he could trust (Job 6:14–15; Job 6:21–23, 27). If they were in a covenant with one another, Job was accusing his friends of violating their covenant with him.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The city of Tema, located in the northern Arabian desert, was at the place roads crossed from Damascus to Mecca and from the Persian Gulf to Aqaba (Isaiah 21:14; Jeremiah 25:23). They might have named it after an ancestor who descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:15). It was different from "Teman," which was Eliphaz’s home in Edom.

• Sheba, situated in southwest Arabia, was a trading city for valuable goods (Psalm 72:10, Psalms 72:15; Isaiah 60:6; Jeremiah 6:20; Ezekiel 27:22–23; Ezekiel 38:13).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: even cast lots for an orphan: Job once protected orphans (Job 31:17, Job 31:21). He used a common saying to show his counselors' lack of compassion for those who had no one to defend them (see Job 17:5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Can my mouth not discern malice?: Job might have been referring to his earlier comment about a "tasteless" and unpleasant diet (Job 6:6–7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Human life has been difficult since the effects of the first human sin (Genesis 3:17; Genesis 5:29; Ecclesiastes 1:2, Ecclesiastes 1:13–14; Ecclesiastes 2:11, Ecclesiastes 2:17; Romans 8:20–22).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Employers had the obligation to pay workers at the end of each day (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:15). But this did not always happen (Jeremiah 22:13; Malachi 3:5; James 5:4).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Job's testing might have lasted for months. 

• The Hebrew word ('amal) appears throughout Job and means "misery" or "miserable" or "trouble" (Job 3:20; Job 11:16; Job 16:2; Job 20:22; Job 3:10; Job 4:8; Job 5:6, Job 5:7; Job 15:35).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's mention of worms symbolized the human fate of death and the widespread corruption in Sheol (Job 25:6; Job 17:14; Job 21:26; Job 24:20; see Isaiah 14:11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job cried out to God, saying life was too short (Job 7:6–10). This complaint contrasts with his earlier wish for God to end his life (Job 6:9).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• People who ask God to remember usually seek his promised mercy (Psalms 35:6; Psalms 106:4).

• Job's statement that life is but a breath (Hebrew ruakh) meant he was either close to death or that life is like the passing of the wind (Psalm 39:9, Psalms 39:11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: You will look for me, but I will be no more: The ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) left out this verse. They did not want to suggest that God could not see Job in Sheol (see study note on 7:9).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
goes down to Sheol: This is the first plain mention of Sheol in Job. 

It is described as: 

• A place of rest from the pressures and distinctions of earth (Job 3:13–19).

• "Darkness" (Job 10:21–22; Job 17:13).

• Deep in the earth (Job 11:8).

• Covered in dust (Job 17:16). 

• The fate of all living beings from which no one can return (Job 30:23; Job 10:21; see Genesis 37:25; 2 Samuel 12:12).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: I will not restrain my mouth: Job echoed Eliphaz's struggle to "keep from speaking" (Job 4:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The sea (Hebrew yam) and the monster (Hebrew tannin) symbolize chaos opposing God's order of creation. In Canaanite mythology, "Yam" was the original sea god, and "Tannin" was a sea monster or a god of the myth of chaos (Jeremiah 51:34; Psalm 74:13–14). This chaos also appears in Job as "Leviathan" or "Rahab" (Job 3:8; Isaiah 27:1; Job 9:13; Job 26:12; Isaiah 51:9). The Lord has total control (sovereignty) over the sea and everything it represents (Job 26:12; Job 38:8–11; Psalm 89:9–10; Jeremiah 5:22).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's dreams and visions while sick were similar to those of Eliphaz (Job 4:12–16).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: for my days are but a breath: Literally for my days are a vapor (Hebrew hebel); see the Theme Note titled “All Is ‘Vapor’.”

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• that You should exalt him: Compare with Psalm 8:4–5, which expresses similar thoughts in a positive way. 

• attend (Hebrew paqad): In Psalm 8:4, this term means "to honor or care for." Job used it ironically to mean "You bother yourself" (compare with "punished," Isaiah 26:14).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Will You never look away from me (literally How long will you not look away from me): Job wanted the opposite of the attention that loyal people usually desire (Numbers 6:25; Psalms 27:9; Psalms 69:17; Psalms 80:3, Psalms 80:7, Psalms 80:19; Lamentations 1:9).

• to swallow: This means “a chance to calm my breathing.”

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Watcher of mankind: Instead of praising God for his goodness shown in careful attention, Job accused God of hostile surveillance. This actually describes Satan's actions (Deuteronomy 32:10; Psalm 25:21; Proverbs 24:12; Job 1:7).

• Why comes from the language of grief (see study note on 3:11–24). 

• Your target: See Job 6:4; Lamentations 3:12.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Like Eliphaz, Bildad the Shuhite thought Job's suffering was God's punishment (see study note on 2:11; Job 8:3–6, Job 8:13; compare Job 4:7–8; Job 5:2–3). Bildad respected the wisdom of the past and spoke to Job with both advice and encouragement (Job 8:8–10; compare Job 4:7; Job 8:3–6, Job 8:8–10; compare Job 4:12–21; Job 5:9–16; Job 8:5–7, Job 8:20–22; compare Job 4:6; Job 5:19–26). He suggested that Job should stop complaining. Bildad advised Job to "ask the Almighty for mercy" and let God's justice restore him (Job 8:1–7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: How long: Bildad might have meant make fun of Job using a similar question (see Job 7:19).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Bildad believed God does not pervert justice. He thought the death of Job’s children showed they had sinned against God. Bildad divided people into "the blameless" (Hebrew tam, Job 8:20a; see Job 1:1) or "the godless" (Hebrew khanep, Job 8:13b). He believed one could distinguish them by observing God's actions toward them.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: your latter days will flourish: Bildad's words were more accurate than he realized (Job 42:12; compare Job 5:19–26).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Bildad argued for traditional wisdom by referring to ancient traditions and history (Deuteronomy 4:32; Jeremiah 18:13).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: born yesterday and know nothing: Bildad suggested that Job's generation was either born too late to know ancient wisdom or too young to have gathered it.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Papyrus reeds can grow as high as three to four and one-half meters (ten to fifteen feet).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: To forget God means behaving as if God does not exist or cannot see (see Psalms 10:4; Psalms 14:1; Zephaniah 1:12; see Job 22:13–17; Psalm 94:7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: In this symbolic story, a plant spreads its shoots over the garden. The roots wrap around the rock heap, giving the plant stability.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
Job answered Bildad by describing God's universal and legal power. His speech resembles a complex legal case. 

It includes: 

• A summons and response (Job 9:3, Job 9:14–16, Job 9:19b, Job 9:32).

• The risk of proving himself guilty (Job 9:20).

• A "mediator" (Job 9:33–34).

• A question of accusation (Job 9:12).

• A legal sentence (Job 9:22).

• A declaration of guilt (Job 9:28–30).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: If one wished to contend with God: Job later wished to meet God in court (Job 13:3, Job 13:15, Job 13:23; Job 23:4).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
When God moves mountains or shakes the earth, it shows his presence as:

• One who gives laws (Exodus 19:18).

• One who judges (Jeremiah 4:24).

• One who rescues (Psalm 18:7; Isaiah 13:13; Isaiah 29:6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Job 38:32 mentions the Bear. It is often identified as "Arcturus." It might also refer to the constellations (star patterns) "Ursa Minor" or "Leo." 

• the Pleiades is a group of seven stars, referenced at Job 38:31 and Amos 5:8.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: the helpers of Rahab: Job described the power of demons as mythical sea monsters that represented chaos. This kind of imagery appears in other parts of the Bible as well (Job 26:12; Psalm 89:11; Isaiah 51:9).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: with a tempest: The words translated as “with a tempest” (bis’arah) might also mean besa‘arah (“for a hair,” meaning “for the smallest thing”). This would parallel "without cause."

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job was truly blameless, and he consistently claimed this during the debate (Job 1:1, Job 1:7; Job 2:3; Job 23:11–12; Job 27:5; Job 31:1–40).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The word "You" shows this is a prayer, even though, "O God," is not plainly stated in Hebrew.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: wash myself: Job talked about using the strongest soap (lye) to represent removing all sin (Job 1:5; compare Psalm 26:6; Matthew 27:24).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The pit can refer to the place of dead people, suggesting the "corruption" of death (Job 17:14; Job 33:18).

• The dirty clothes representing being guilty contrast with the clean clothes representing being innocent (Zechariah 3:3–5; see Isaiah 61:10; Isaiah 64:6; Revelation 19:8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: A mediator does not judge God and man. Instead, the mediator helps bring them together (see Job 16:19–21).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• A series of images shows God's role in creating Job. 

• Your hands shaped me … You molded me like clay: This is how a "potter" makes a vessel (Isaiah 45:9; Jeremiah 18:1–12). Although the potter has complete control over the clay, Job still questioned God (Isaiah 45:9; Jeremiah 18:5–12; Romans 9:20–25).

• return me to dust: This common theme in Job shows life's temporary nature (Job 4:19; Job 7:9–10, Job 7:21; Job 14:1–2, Job 14:10; see Genesis 3:19).

• You not pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese: The Hebrew terms create a lively image of a new born baby still covered with vernix (a creamy substance).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Earlier, Job described "Sheol" as a somewhat peaceful place (Job 3:13–19). Now, he calls it a land of darkness and gloom (see also Job 7:9–10; Job 14:7–22).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Zophar the Naamathite, the most harsh of Job’s three friends, focused only on the issue of sin (see study note on 2:11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• This stream of words: Those who are foolish and those who sin often talk too much, but Job was innocent (Proverbs 10:8, Job 10:14; Proverbs 10:19).

• Will you scoff without rebuke?: Zophar thought Job's comments were full of sin because he was making fun of God's justice (Job 10:2–7, Job 10:13–15).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: My doctrine is sound: Job was not defining doctrine but was defending his own integrity.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: exacts from you less than your iniquity deserves: Zophar believed that disasters were God's punishment for sins (compare Job 34:36).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: discover the limits of the Almighty: No one can fully understand the Almighty, who is beyond the heavens, the place of dead people, the land, and the sea (Job 11:8–9).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
Zophar outlined three conditions for restoration (Job 11:15): 

• Direct your heart. This is an internal action beyond mere ceremony.

• Lift up your hands. This is a symbolic gesture of prayer, appeal, or act of surrendering (Exodus 9:29; Proverbs 1:24; Isaiah 1:15).

• Put away the iniquity. This is not through sacrifice and regret, but by quitting the sin in view (compare Hebrews 11:6; James 4:8; James 5:16).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: In his longest speech so far, Job responds to Zophar's comments and the entire first round of speeches.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: ask the animals … the birds … the earth … the fish: Job believed the reason for his grief was obvious and that even creation would understand it (Proverbs 6:6). Later, God directed Job to the animal kingdom to show him that he did not understand (Job 38–40).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The change from you (plural in Job 12:2–3) to you (singular here) probably indicates that Job is speaking to Zophar.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: the hand of the LORD: This is the only place in the dialogues where the Hebrew name, "Yahweh" (“the LORD”), appears (chapters Job 3:3–27; Job 29:29–37). For Job, the issue was not who caused his grief but why it happened.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: the tongue tastes its food: See Job 6:6–7.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Wisdom is found with the elderly: People often think wisdom comes with old age. Job's friends supported this idea but Job doubted it (Job 8:8–10; Job 15:10; Job 32:6–9; Job 12:20).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: He leads counselors away barefoot: In this metaphor, God removes leaders' abilities. It could also mean losing the symbols of office or becoming naked captives (Job 12:18–19).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: When God removes the royal robe of kings, he takes away their symbols of authority (compare Job 19:9). It can also mean "God loosens the bonds of kings," referring to the control they have imposed on others.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The priests lose their status or their priestly robes. They might even be naked captives (Job 12:18).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Pours out contempt on nobles: Compare Psalm 107:40.

• disarms the mighty (literally loosens the belt of): The strong are not ready for battle anymore.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• He reveals the deep things: This phrase might refer to Zophar’s words that God’s knowledge is "deeper than Sheol" (Job 11:8). 

• darkness … deep shadows: The Old Testament often describes God as living in darkness and showing himself through darkness (1 Kings 8:12; 2 Chronicles 6:1; 2 Samuel 22:10, 2 Samuel 22:12; Psalm 18:9, Psalms 18:11). Examples are when he gave the law at Sinai or when he comes in judgment (Deuteronomy 4:11; Deuteronomy 5:22–23; Zephaniah 1:15).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Compare Daniel 2:21. 

• He deprives the earth’s leaders of reason: See Job 12:18; compare Daniel 4:23, Daniel 4:32–33. 

• He… makes them wander in a trackless wasteland: This is like the "nobles" in Psalm 107:40 (see Job 12:21).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Lack of wise advice might have caused the kings to stagger like drunkards (Job 12:17; see Isaiah 19:14). This happened because they experienced God's punishment (Psalm 75:8; Jeremiah 25:15–27).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job appealed to experience, just like his comforters had done (Job 3:12–17; Job 5:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Will you speak wickedly on God’s behalf: False witnesses were not allowed, even when speaking for God (Exodus 20:16).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Ashes have no value (see Isaiah 44:20).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job thought about finding a judge to remove God's burden from him (Job 9:33–34). Eliphaz had encouraged Job to accept God's discipline (Job 5:17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job wanted God to call or summon him, so Job could defend himself. Or as an alternative, Job would speak to God. Then God would respond with the charges against Job. Since God did not choose the first option, Job started the second one (Job 13:23). Eventually, God did call Job (Job 38:1–3; Job 40:1–2). But Job could not reply (Job 40:3–5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• God can turn away in "anger"(Deuteronomy 31:18; Isaiah 54:8; Jeremiah 33:5). Or he can choose not to show friendship (Psalms 30:7; Psalms 69:17; Psalms 102:2).

• Job, perhaps making a play of words on his own name (’iyyob), denied being God's enemy (’oyeb).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: In the Old Testament, dry chaff often symbolizes something that can blow away or burn (Psalm 83:13; Isaiah 40:24; Jeremiah 13:24; Exodus 15:7; Isaiah 47:14; Malachi 4:1; see also “dry grass,” Isaiah 5:24; Isaiah 33:11). It also represents weakness and lack of importance (Job 41:20–21; Isaiah 41:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The flower symbolizes how short life is (Psalms 90:5–6; Psalms 103:15–16; Isaiah 40:6–7). 

• A shadow passes quickly (1 Chronicles 29:15; Psalm 102:11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: open Your eyes: Job complained about God's constant surveillance (Job 7:8, Job 7:17–20; Job 10:6, Job 10:14; Job 13:27).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: does not rise: Job did not have even the minimal evidence of resurrection found in the Old Testament (2 Kings 13:21; Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2; see also Job 19:25). Job was not focusing on the end of the universe when the heavens will disappear (Psalm 102:25–26; Isaiah 34:4; Isaiah 51:6; Hebrews 1:10–12). He was referring to the eternal nature of the heavens (Psalm 148:6; see also Psalms 72:5, Psalms 72:7, Psalms 72:17; Psalms 89:29, Psalms 89:37). His phrase refers to the permanent state of death.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The grave is a permanent home (Job 14:10–12, see Job 3:13–19; Job 7:6–10; Job 10:20–22). Job could not fulfill his request from Job 13:20–21 to hide temporarily in the grave.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: count my steps: Here, Job refers to God's protective care rather than his surveillance (Job 10:12; Job 13:27; Job 14:3).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: If transgression becomes sealed in a bag, it does not wait for judgment (Deuteronomy 32:34–35; Hosea 13:12). It remains hidden forever. Job was asking for God to forgive him.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job no longer considered Sheol as a safe place (Job 3:17–19; Job 14:13–17). The Old Testament often describes dead people as having no feelings (Psalm 88:12; Ecclesiastes 9:5; compare Isaiah 50:11; Isaiah 66:24). The New Testament more plainly teaches that evil dead people experience suffering (Luke 16:23, Luke 16:28; Revelation 14:11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: In this second round of speeches, Job's friends discuss the fate of wicked people. They suggest that Job's condition means he has sinned.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: fill his belly with the hot east wind: The east wind was hot, so it might symbolize upset or violent speech (Exodus 14:21; Hosea 13:15; Jonah 4:8; Job 27:21; Jeremiah 18:17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Your own mouth … condemns you: Job feared this would happen (Job 9:20; see Matthew 26:65).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: When the Lord later gave a similar challenge, Job found it convincing (Job 38:1–11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The book's readers know about God's secret council (Job 1:6–12; Job 2:1–6; see 1 Kings 22:19–20; Psalm 89:5–7). But Job and his friends did not.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Aged men who are gray-haired claim they alone have wisdom (Job 8:8–10; Job 12:20; see Job 12:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: why do your eyes flash: This sentence might be a metaphor for unbelief, or it could mean winking like a person planning a trick or someone blinking in disbelief.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• What is man, that he should be pure: Eliphaz repeated himself and Job (Job 4:17–19; Job 7:17; Job 14:4).

• one born of woman: Both man and born of woman suggest weakness.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The heavens, often linked with what is pure, were not completely pure (Exodus 24:10). Rebellious angels may have brought pollution (Job 1:6–7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: when no foreigner passed among them: Eliphaz's contempt for foreign ideas is ironic. Wisdom literature is more international than other Old Testament writings.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
Evil people experience everything that happened to Job (see Job 1:16–19):

• Attacks by thieves (Job 15:21).

• Loss of possessions (Job 15:29).

• Collapse of houses (Job 15:28).

• Fire (Job 15:30, Job 15:34).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Eliphaz spoke about the fear that evil people feel, and Job had similar experiences (Job 3:25; Job 6:4; Job 9:34; Job 13:11, Job 13:21; Job 23:15; Job 27:20; Job 30:15). Bildad and Zophar warned of more fear to come (Job 18:11,14; 20:25). 

• The Sabeans and Chaldeans were examples of "destroyers" (Job 1:13–17). But this could mean any destructive force (Job 1:18–19). A destroyer might be an agent of Satan or divine agents that punish evil (1 Corinthians 10:10; Revelation 9:11; Exodus 12:23; 2 Samuel 24:16; 2 Chronicles 32:21; Acts 12:23; Hebrews 11:28). Eliphaz referred to divine agents.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: he is marked for the sword: The evil people may die by murder or by God's punishment.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Like evil people, Job may have experienced hunger. Or, following the ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), the Berean Standard Bible says Job "wanders about as food for vultures.” This would be similar to being “marked for the sword” (Job 15:22).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Earlier, Job complained that God was treating him like a powerful enemy (Job 7:19–21; Job 13:24).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The flame, could refer to the sun burning or the flame of judgment from God (see Job 15:34; Numbers 16:31–35; Psalms 106:17–18; Ezekiel 20:47). 

• the breath of God's mouth: This might be a desert wind or a direct "theophany" (a revelation of God’s presence) that caused the "fire" of Job 15:34.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: "The flame" of judgment will destroy the unfair profits of those without faith (Job 15:30).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job might have wanted to shake his head in to make fun or in horror (2 Kings 19:21; Psalms 22:7; Psalms 109:25; Isaiah 37:22; Jeremiah 18:16; Lamentations 2:15; Matthew 27:39).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's family includes by extension his household and his servants (Job 1:15–19).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• They open their mouths against me: Job was mocked (compare Psalm 35:21; Isaiah 57:4; Lamentations 2:16; Lamentations 3:46).

• strike my cheeks: This was more of an insult than an act of violence (Psalm 3:7; Micah 5:1; see also 1 Kings 22:24; Isaiah 50:6; Lamentations 3:30; Matthew 26:67).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: He seized me by the neck: This might refer to a wild animal capturing its prey (see Job 16:9). However, it is more likely a military image signaling defeat (Genesis 49:8; Psalm 18:40).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: my gall: This describes injuries to important organs.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: He breaks me with wound upon wound: Job imagines himself as a defensive military station with God attacking. Job regarded God as a warrior who neither defended nor saved him (see Exodus 15:3; Psalm 24:8; see Jeremiah 20:11; Zephaniah 3:17). Instead, God attacked him as if he were a threat (see Job 6:12; Isaiah 42:13).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Since Job insisted he was innocent, wearing sackcloth showed grief, not asking God to forgive him. He might have worn it to show he would never take it off because no one could comfort him (Genesis 37:34–35).

• I have buried my horn in the dust: A horn symbolized dignity and power (1 Samuel 2:1; Psalms 75:4–5; Psalms 89:17, Psalms 89:24; Psalms 92:10; Psalms 112:9; Psalms 148:14). Cutting it off caused deep humiliation (Psalm 75:10; Jeremiah 48:25; Zechariah 1:12).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Free of violence (Hebrew lo’-khamas): If violence is the meaning, Job might have been denying that he was a dangerous warrior who God should attack (Job 16:12–14; see also Isaiah 59:6; Jonah 3:8).

• Contrary to Eliphaz’s accusation and Bildad’s assumption, Job’s prayer was sincere because he was innocent (Job 15:4–5; Job 8:6; Genesis 20:5; Isaiah 59:3).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's blood would testify that he was innocent and suffered without cause (compare Genesis 4:10–11; Isaiah 26:21; Ezekiel 24:7–8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job thought his suffering would lead to his death (Job 7:7, Job 7:21; Job 10:20–22). He asked God to show his innocence, even if he died before that happened.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: my witness is in heaven: Job wished for a kind third party to be "a mediator" between him and God (see Job 9:32–35). Job wanted a heavenly advocate who would eventually stand on the earth (Job 16:19; compare Zechariah 3:1; Job 19:25; compare 1 Samuel 24:15; John 14:16, John 14:26; John 15:26; John 16:7; 1 John 2:1).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: My spirit is broken: This can mean a truly sorry attitude (Psalm 51:17). But it usually means a very sad "spirit" (Proverbs 18:14).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: mockers surround me: songs of grief (laments) often describe making fun of someone as how evil people respond to the suffering of righteous people (Psalms 22:7; Psalms 69:10–12; Psalms 89:50–52). In wisdom literature, people make fun of right behavior (Proverbs 1:22; Proverbs 9:7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Give me, I pray, the pledge You demand (literally please keep my pledge with yourself): A pledge (Hebrew ‘erabon) can be a deposit that guarantees payment (Genesis 38:17–20; Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:10–14; see Proverbs 20:16; Proverbs 27:13). So, this might suggest God forgiving sin (making atonement). It might also refer to Job’s wish for an advocate to support his cause (see study note on Job 16:19–21).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Spitting in someone's face was more insulting than a slap because it made the person ceremonially unclean (Job 16:10; Numbers 12:14).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Some scholars think these verses are out of place. However, Job might have been quoting his opponents' words ironically.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job no longer trusted his friends and thought he would die without hope (Job 6:15–21; Job 13:4–5; Job 16:2–3; compare Job 12:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: for Sheol: People imagined the realm of dead people as a home (Job 30:23; Psalm 49:11; Ecclesiastes 12:5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: my father … mother … sister: This sad imitation of a family gathering in a cemetery shows how Job imagined his coming death.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: the gates of Sheol: Sheol is the place where dead people reside. Ancient people thought it had a gate with bars that allowed no escape.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: How long until you end these speeches?: Bildad spoke to Job as if addressing a group, possibly meaning "people like you."

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The phrase, "the lamp of the wicked is extinguished," might symbolize a life filled with confusion and darkness (Proverbs 4:19). More likely, it suggests an early death (Proverbs 13:9; Proverbs 24:20).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: A shortened stride is the opposite of walking and running in a life of blessings (Proverbs 4:12).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: A series of devices for hunting shows the biblical principle of revenge (see study note on 34:11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Bildad uses the biblical idea of revenge (consequences for doing wrong) in Job's case, as do Eliphaz and Zophar.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: death devours: The prophet Isaiah later changed this image. He pictured the Lord as defeating death (Isaiah 25:8; see 1 Corinthians 15:54).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The image of burning sulfur reminds the reader of what happened to Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24). It suggests what will happen to all evil people (Psalm 11:6; Revelation 19:20; Revelation 21:8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: People often speak against (curse) evil people by saying that future generations will forget their memory (see Job 18:19; Psalms 34:16; Psalms 109:13; Proverbs 10:7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: This bad fortune (curse) of Job no longer having children and Bildad’s earlier cruel acts show that he believed Job's suffering was a fair punishment because he did wrong (see Job 18:16; Psalms 109:13; Isaiah 14:21–22; Job 8:4; Job 1:18–19).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: in the west … in the east: These phrases might refer to people from the past and future or from different places.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Bildad kept implying that Job had rejected God (Job 15:4, Job 15:13, Job 15:25).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The number ten symbolized a large, non-definite quantity rather than a specific count (for example, Genesis 31:7; Leviticus 26:26; Numbers 14:22; Daniel 1:20).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Job believed justice delayed and that God was unfair it how he had treated him (Job 19:7; Job 19:8–12). Later, Elihu and God disagreed (Job 34:12; Job 40:2).

• drawn His net around me: Job might have been replying to Bildad’s accusation (Job 18:8–10).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Violence!: Compare Jeremiah 20:8; Habakkuk 1:2–3.

• no response: See Psalm 22:2; Lamentations 3:8; Habakkuk 1:2–3.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: has blocked my way: See Job 3:23; Job 13:27; Psalm 88:8; Lamentations 3:7, Lamentations 3:9.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: has stripped me of my honor: See Job 12:17–19; Job 29:7–14, Job 29:20.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: my own family: Job might have meant his tribe, his parents, his children, or his siblings.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: those I love have turned against me: See Job 2:11; also Job 6:14–15, Job 6:21–23, Job 6:27; compare Psalms 41:9; Psalms 55:12–14, Psalms 55:20.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: escaped by the skin of my teeth: This figure of speech means a narrow escape. In Hebrew, it might also suggest that Job became as thin as a skeleton with a skull full of teeth.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: the hand of God has struck me: God allowed Satan to harm Job (Job 1:11; Job 2:5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: persecute (literally pursue): Job said that God followed him like a someone hunting or a warrior (Job 10:16; Job 16:13).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job wanted his words inscribed (carved) on a monument, not in a book. He wanted a record of his innocence that would last in response to Bildad's claim that he would become forgotten (Job 18:17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
Job's faith in a Redeemer (one who saves) could only become fulfilled in Christ. This was also true for his wish for an advocate and a witness in heaven (Job 9:33; Job 16:19). The term Redeemer (Hebrew go’el) comes from both criminal and civil law. A person could redeem or take revenge because of the wrong shedding of blood or redeem lost property. This included buying back a slave or marrying the widow who inherited the property (Numbers 35:12–18; Leviticus 25:25, Leviticus 25:47–49; Leviticus 27:11–13; Ruth 3:13). 

The Old Testament recognized the Lord as Redeemer (Exodus 6:6; Psalms 19:14; Psalms 103:4; Proverbs 23:10–11; Isaiah 43:1; Isaiah 54:5). New Testament Christians know the Redeemer as the Lord Jesus Christ (Ephesians 1:7, Ephesians 1:14; Hebrews 9:12; 1 Peter 1:18). Job wanted his Redeemer to declare his innocence (see Job 1:1 and corresponding study note).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job believed God would prove him right, even if he died first.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: I will see Him for myself: This thought is like the psalmist's in "when I awake" (Psalm 17:15). For Job, this hope could only come true by seeing God at the end of time when his body transformed (Matthew 5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 John 3:2; Revelation 1:7; 1 Corinthians 15:43–53; Philippians 3:21).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: According to biblical principles against lying, Job warned his friends to fear God's judgment (Job 13:7–11; see Matthew 7:1–2; James 4:11–12). They eventually encountered his judgment, but they also received mercy (Job 42:7–8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: he will perish forever, like his own dung: Compare 1 Kings 14:9–11; 2 Kings 9:36–37; Psalm 83:10; Jeremiah 8:1–2.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Riches stolen do not provide benefits that last because they obtain them in a dishonest way (Job 20:18–21).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: venom of cobras … poison of cobras … vipers: In the end, evil people harm only themselves, not others (Matthew 3:7; Romans 3:13; Proverbs 23:29–35).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The streams of olive oil and rivers flowing with honey and cream represent great blessings (Exodus 5:19; Deuteronomy 27:3; Joel 3:18).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Like the grave or death, evil people always focus on themselves and never find satisfaction (Proverbs 27:20; Proverbs 30:15–16; Ecclesiastes 5:19; Isaiah 57:20–21; Habakkuk 2:5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Evil people cannot avoid trouble (see Isaiah 24:17–18; Jeremiah 15:2–3; Amos 5:19; Amos 9:1–2). When they escape one threat, another confronts them.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Terrors: These are terrors of death. Although the specific words "of death" are not in the Hebrew text, they are understood because the description talks about an arrowhead that glistens with blood (literally with gall). This indicates a deadly hit on an important organ in the body (Job 6:4; Job 16:13; Psalm 7:12). The image conveys the serious threat and intense fear that comes with being in mortal danger.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Images like darkness and fire often symbolize God's presence, especially his judgment (Deuteronomy 4:11; Deuteronomy 5:22–23; Hebrews 12:18; Exodus 9:23–24; Exodus 10:21–29).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The heavens … will rise up: Compare Deuteronomy 4:26; Deuteronomy 30:19; Deuteronomy 31:28.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job’s friends claimed they were delivering God’s message of consolation or comfort. But Job found no comfort in their words. He asked them to comfort him by giving him silent attention (Job 15:11; Job 16:2; Job 13:5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• When I think about what I am saying: Job felt upset about his horrible task of complaining against God and talking about his terrors (Job 13:3, Job 13:15–16, Job 13:22; Job 23:1–5; Job 6:4; Job 27:20; Job 30:15).

• my body trembles: This reaction is similar to that of the prophets Habakkuk, Ezekiel, and Daniel (Habakkuk 1:5; Habakkuk 3:16; Ezekiel 3:14; Daniel 8:27; Daniel 10:8–9).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Despite what Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar claimed, Job observed that evil people have children and grandchildren (Job 5:4); Job 18:19; Job 20:10). These should be rewards for righteous people (Proverbs 17:6). But Job felt they would not be his reward (Job 1:18–19; see also Job 42:13–16).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: the lamp of the wicked put out: Job disagreed with Bildad and the standard perspective of wisdom (Job 18:5–6, Job 18:18; Proverbs 13:9; Proverbs 20:20; Job 24:20; see God’s comments at Job 38:15).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• It is said: Job was quoting and responding to his friends' arguments. 

• God lays up one’s punishment for his children: Eliphaz and Zophar said this, but Job believed God should punish the people who sin (Job 5:4; Job 20:10; see Ezekiel 18:19–20).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• This question assumes the answer that no one can teach God a lesson (Isaiah 40:13–14; Isaiah 45:9; Romans 11:34; 1 Corinthians 2:16).

• The phrase those on high might refer to good or bad angels (demons) (1 Corinthians 6:3; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 1:6; Revelation 20:1–3). Or, more likely, it refers to powerful people on earth (Job 34:17–19).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: his bones are rich with marrow: People once believed bones were the source of health.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: in the bitterness of his soul: Job often complained about how life seemed useless (Job 3:20; Job 7:11; Job 9:18; Job 10:1).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: worms cover them both: Compare Job 17:14; Isaiah 14:11; see Job 19:26.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: where are the tents in which the wicked dwell: Job was echoing the words of Bildad, Eliphaz and Zophar (Job 8:22; Job 15:34; Job 20:26).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The clods of the valley are sweet to him: Job considered death as a relief (Job 3:17–18).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: They told lies about Job and God (Job 13:4; Job 42:7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: In this third round of speeches, Job's friends plainly accuse him of being evil and sharing the fate of those who do evil.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Eliphaz did not understand that God would delight in Job’s right relationship with him, just as God does with every righteous person (Job 1:8; Job 2:3; 1 Chronicles 29:17; Psalms 147:10–11; Proverbs 11:1, Proverbs 11:20; Proverbs 12:22). God would also benefit from Job’s steady faith, which exposed the lie in Satan’s challenge (Job 1:9–12; Job 2:4–6).

• Job firmly claimed that he was blameless (Job 23:10–12). God said the same thing (Job 1:1, Job 1:8; Job 2:3).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The law and prophets forbade taking clothing as security for loans (Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:10–13; Ezekiel 18:7–8; Amos 2:8). In contrast, Job gave clothing to poor people (Job 31:19–20).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The Old Testament assigns Israel the duty of caring for widows and the fatherless (Deuteronomy 10:18; Deuteronomy 14:29). It often condemns neglecting them as the worst evil against society (Exodus 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 27:19). Job agreed that neglecting them was wrong but claimed he was innocent (Job 24:3, Job 24:21; Job 29:12–13; Job 31:16–18, Job 31:21).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: What does God know?: Job did not claim that God cannot see, but others have (see Psalms 10:11; Psalms 73:11; Psalms 94:7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: so I stay far from the counsel of the wicked: Eliphaz repeated Job’s words to him (Job 21:16b).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The righteous see it and are glad: Those in a right relationship with God will be glad to see justice done and wrong things made right (see also Psalm 58:10–11; Revelation 19:1–4). Eliphaz's perspective overlooked God's wish "that the wicked should turn from their ways and live" (see Ezekiel 33:11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The term instruction (Hebrew torah, also meaning "law," Deuteronomy 17:11), used in Job only here, often refers to the "Pentateuch" (Genesis through Deuteronomy). 

• Receive … lay up: See Deuteronomy 4:1–2; Deuteronomy 6:6–9; Psalm 119:11; Proverbs 2:1–9. Job had done this thing (Job 23:12).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: return to the Almighty: Bildad and Zophar had already made a wrong application of this principle of the Bible (Job 8:5–6; Job 11:13–14; Isaiah 55:6–7; Hosea 14:1–2; Zechariah 1:3; Acts 26:20). Now Eliphaz also makes a wrong application of it.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: gold of Ophir: Ophir was probably in southern Arabia (see 1 Kings 9:28; 1 Kings 22:48). The gold of Ophir set the standard for fine gold (Isaiah 13:12). Queens wore it at weddings (Psalm 45:9).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: God promises to be a "treasure" for his people (Psalm 16:5; Isaiah 33:6; Matthew 19:21; Mark 10:21). Even if they own nothing, they will be "rich" (2 Corinthians 6:10; James 2:5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Ironically, Job will pray, God will hear, and Eliphaz will benefit (Job 42:8).

• you will fulfill your vows: People often vowed after God forgave them (Hosea 14:2; Jonah 1:16; Jonah 2:9). They also vowed when asking help from God (Judges 11:29–40; 1 Samuel 1:1–28). Vows mean a serious commitments or to swear a promise (Numbers 30:2; Deuteronomy 23:23; Psalms 22:25; Psalms 61:5, Psalms 61:8; Psalms 116:14, Psalms 116:18; Ecclesiastes 5:4–5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: This difficult text probably shows how effective the prayer of a person in a right relationship with God can be. The idea appears throughout the Bible (Psalms 34:15, Psalms 34:17; Psalms 145:18; Proverbs 15:8, Job 15:29; James 5:16; see also Genesis 18:23–32; Genesis 19:29; Genesis 20:7, Genesis 20:17; Genesis 32:28; Exodus 9:28–32; Exodus 17:11; Exodus 32:10–14; Romans 5:19).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job released his earlier doubts (Job 9:14–20, Job 9:32). Now he expresses confidence that he could present his complaint to God with success.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: plead my case: Job wanted to present his legal case to God (Job 13:3, Job 13:18, Job 13:22; Job 16:21; Job 31:35). Abraham pleaded directly with God about Sodom (Genesis 18:25–32). Moses did the same for Israel (Exodus 32:12–13; Numbers 14:13–19).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Earlier, Job thought God was too powerful for him to "summon" (Job 9:19). He asked for "a mediator" and requested that God not "frighten" him (Job 9:33–34; Job 13:21). Here, he showed more hope that God would give him a fair legal hearing. 

• delivered: Job wanted God to declare him innocent, not forgive him as if he were guilty (Job 13:18; see Psalms 17:2–3; Psalms 26:1–3).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: has tested me: Job did not want the kind of punishment that would make him clean as through "a refiner’s fire" (Proverbs 17:3; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:2–3). He wanted a test to show he was already as pure as gold and did not need to change his life (Job 22:23).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: No one can change God's mind (Job 9:12–13; Job 11:10; Job 12:14; Job 34:29; Numbers 23:19–20; James 1:17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Terrified in His presence: See Psalms 77:3; Psalms 88:16; Psalms 119:120.

• Job had earlier complained about being in darkness (Job 19:8). Eliphaz and Bildad said this fate is for the evil person (Job 15:22; Job 22:1; Job 18:6, Job 18:18).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: reserve times: God sets times for judgment (Ecclesiastes 3:17; Ecclesiastes 8:6; Daniel 2:21; Luke 21:22–24). But we do not know when they are (Acts 1:7). He will reveal them at the right time (1 Thessalonians 5:1–28; 1 Timothy 6:15).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The books of the law, wisdom literature, and prophecy all condemned moving markers of boundaries (Deuteronomy 19:14; Deuteronomy 27:17; Proverbs 22:28; Proverbs 23:10; see study note on Hosea 5:10).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: This list of criminal behaviors first emphasizes crimes against weak people (Job 24:2–12). Then it examines the criminals themselves (Job 24:13–17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The law prohibited taking essential possessions as security or a down payment for a loan (Job 22:6–9; Deuteronomy 24:6, Deuteronomy 24:10–13, Deuteronomy 24:17–21).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: glean the vineyards of the wicked: Job described the desperate situation of poor people. If someone stole their fields like in the case of Naboth's vineyard, the poor person would harvest for the thieves instead of for themselves (Job 24:2; see 1 Kings 21:1–29). They would only get the bits that remained. If the poor had to glean from fields of the wicked people, they would receive nothing (Leviticus 19:10; Leviticus 23:22). But if they would try to gather from the fields of just people, they would be something left for them (Leviticus 19:9–10; Leviticus 23:22; Ruth 2:1–23).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Those who did not lend fairly sometimes took the clothing or blankets of those in debt as a security for the loan. This left those in debt without proper clothing or covering (Job 22:6; Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:11–13; Amos 2:8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: the nursing child of the poor is seized for a debt: See 2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5:1–5; Matthew 18:25.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Forcing workers to tread the winepresses while they go thirsty violates the principle of letting workers enjoy some of the produce they are harvesting (see Deuteronomy 25:4; compare 2 Timothy 2:6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: yet God charges no one with wrongdoing: Job thought that, unlike God's usual character, God did not help those treated wrong or stop evil people from hurting their victims (Exodus 2:23–24; Psalm 12:5; Job 24:2–12; Job 24:13–17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: These ideas seem to go against Job's observations. Some scholars think Bildad or Zophar might have said them. However, Job might have been speaking against evil people, making fun of his friends' opinions by quoting them. Or he might have meant that the fate of evil people also affects those in a right relationship with God. His friends described this earlier (Job 5:2–7; Job 15:17–25; Job 8:8–19; Job 18:5–21; Job 20:4–29; Job 21:23–26).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Eliphaz stated that being innocent or pure is almost impossible (Job 4:17–19; Job 15:14–16). A person can achieve it only after suffering (Job 22:21–23). Bildad argued that only those who are completely blameless can hope to be pure (Job 8:20).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job’s friends did not help him (Job 12:2; Job 16:4). Bildad's claim that innocence was impossible upset Job deeply (Job 10:1–7; Job 13:3, Job 13:13–19; Job 16:18–21; Job 19:23–27; Job 23:2–7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Eliphaz, Zophar, and Elihu all claimed that the right spirit was guiding them (Job 4:15; Job 20:3; Job 32:18; Job 33:4; see also Jeremiah 29:8–9; 1 Corinthians 12:10; 1 John 4:1).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The Hebrew word, Sheol, is where all dead people go. It is beneath the waters.

• The Hebrew word, Abaddon, is the place where evil people go to their destruction.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The Hebrew word tsapon means north. It sometimes refers to the northern mountain of the Canaanite gods, similar to Mount Olympus (Genesis 13:14). The Berean Standard Bible refers to it as the sky, stretched over empty space (see Genesis 1:6–8; Psalm 104:2–3; Isaiah 40:22–23).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: has inscribed a horizon: See Genesis 1:6–10; Psalm 104:6–9; Proverbs 8:29.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: People once believed that mountains at the edge of the horizon were the foundations or "pillars" of heaven or the earth (Judges 16:25–26;Job 9:6). They thought these mountains extended from beneath the sea's waters up to the clouds, supporting the dome of the heavens (Jonah 2:6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• He stirred the sea (compare Exodus 14:21; Mark 4:39; compare Isaiah 51:15; Jeremiah 31:35). God performed a miracle for his people. 

• He shattered Rahab: God showed control over the sea symbolized as a monster ("Rahab"), challenging myths about the sea being divine. See also Psalms 74:13–14; Psalms 89:9–10; Isaiah 27:1; Isaiah 51:9–10.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• His breath (or wind): God's authority clears the skies after a storm (Job 26:12). 

• The fleeing serpent relates to "Yam" and "Rahab" (see study note on 7:12). It provides background for the image of Satan as a "dragon" (Isaiah 27:1; also Psalm 74:13–14; see Genesis 3:15; Romans 16:20; Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job continued his discourse: He no longer responded to his three friends. Instead, he returned to the themes of his opening statement (Job 3:1–26).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The Bible allows for making a vow to the living God (Ruth 3:13; 1 Samuel 20:21; 1 Samuel 25:26; 1 Kings 17:1; 1 Kings 18:15; Jeremiah 4:2). But sometimes people make silly or false vows (1 Samuel 14:39, 1 Samuel 14:45; Jeremiah 5:2). 

• Elihu later criticized Job for claiming that God deprived me of justice (Job 34:5).

• embittered my soul (Job 7:11; Job 10:1; Job 21:25): Compare Naomi and the widow from Shunem after losing her son (Ruth 1:20–21; 2 Kings 4:27).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job found it wrong and offensive to admit that his friends were correct. It was a terrible act to condemn an innocent man like him (Exodus 23:7; Proverbs 6:16–19; Proverbs 17:15).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Some interpreters think this is a new speech by Zophar. Without it, Zophar has no speech in this cycle.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: This section is an isolated speech. There is no speaker listed, so it might continue from earlier words. Some see it as a creative summary by the author of Job. It emphasizes the limits of human wisdom and sets the stage for the Lord's speeches.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: People who mined would melt rock by burning a fire in a mine for days or weeks to extract the solid matter (ore). Some used fire and then cold water to crack the rocks.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Wisdom does not come from people. God is the true source of wisdom (Job 28:23–28).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The metals, gems, and glass listed here were valuable in the ancient world. However, the speaker says wisdom is more valuable than wealth.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: When God looks across the entire earth, he sees his wisdom in his creation (Job 28:23). God later showed his wisdom to Job by taking him on a tour of the universe (chapters Job 38:38–41).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: the fear of the Lord (Hebrew, ’adonay): In the book of Job, this name for God appears only here. This might suggest that chapter Job 28:28 is a poem by the person narrating.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job compares his past happiness, honor, and wealth with his current loss of social dignity and divine friendship (chapters Job 29:29 and Job 30:30). He ends his speech with broad vows of innocence (chapter Job 31:31).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: In other parts of the text, Job uses the Hebrew word shamar to describe what he sees as God's severe surveillance (Job 10:14; Job 13:27; Job 14:16). However, here it refers to God's kind care, meaning watched over (Psalm 121:3–8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The city gate served as the town's administrative center (see Ruth 4:1–2, Ruth 4:11).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job described his righteousness using royal imagery. In the Bible, a robe often symbolizes righteousness (Psalm 132:9; Isaiah 59:17; Isaiah 61:10; Romans 13:14; Revelation 19:8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job was active in searching out and helping strangers in need.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: and multiply my days as the sand (literally after I have counted my days like sand): Job believed the length of his years showed God's blessing. This was similar to the numerous people descended from Abraham or the abundance of supplies Joseph had in Egypt (Genesis 15:5; Genesis 32:12; Genesis 41:49).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: In the past, Job was a comforter of the mourners (Job 4:3–4). This verse is a prophetic command closely linked to the work of the Christ (Isaiah 40:1; Isaiah 61:1–3; Luke 4:18–19; see also 2 Corinthians 1:3–4).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: In the past, the most important members of society praised Job (Job 29:11). Now, the least important made fun of him and spit in his face (Job 30:1, 10). Compare with Psalms 35:15; Psalms 69:12; Mark 14:65; Mark 15:17–20.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
They live in scary valleys (wadis), caves (holes), and among rocks. 

The miserable life of those making fun of Job was like: 

• Israel’s situation under Midianite abuse (Judges 6:2).

• David’s life when he fled from King Saul (1 Samuel 22:1–2).

• The prophet Elijah’s life as he waited for the Lord’s instruction (1 Kings 17:3–8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: they mock me: See also Job 17:6; compare with Psalm 69:12; Lamentations 3:14, Lamentations 3:63.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• keep far from me: See also Job 19:13–15; compare Psalm 88:8; Proverbs 19:7; Matthew 26:56.

• Spitting in someone's face showed extreme dislike or hatred (Deuteronomy 25:9; Isaiah 50:6; Matthew 26:67; Matthew 27:30; Mark 14:65).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The series of images here shows a military attack on a city with strong defenses. Job had already used this image to describe God's attack on him (Job 19:10–12).

• The word translated as snares might refer to ramps raised against a city's walls. A siege ramp was a large sloped structure of earth and stones that armies built against city walls. These ramps allowed attacking soldiers to climb up to the top of the walls during a battle.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Terrors: See also Job 6:4; Job 7:14; compare with Psalm 88:15.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: He seizes me by the collar: The Hebrew in this verse is hard to translate. It might mean Job feels like God is choking him and he is a throw him into the mud (compare Job 30:19).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: dust and ashes: Earlier, Job sat among the ashes in pain (Job 2:8). Later, he would sit in dust and ashes to "repent" (Job 42:6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: You do not answer: Job often complained about this (Job 9:16; Job 19:7; Job 23:2–9; Job 31:35). But God soon responded (Job 38:1).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job felt like he was caught in a storm and blown around like useless "straw" or "chaff" (Job 9:17; Job 21:18; Job 27:21; Psalm 1:4; Isaiah 17:13).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Before his testing began, people respected Job in the public square (Job 29:7–10, Job 29:21–25). He helped those in need (Job 29:11–17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job might have been expressing how he saw himself, how others saw him, or both. By saying he was a brother of jackals, a companion to owls, Job might have been describing his deep grief (Micah 1:8). People associated jackals with things devastated or ruins (see Psalm 63:10; Isaiah 13:22; Isaiah 34:13; Isaiah 35:7; Jeremiah 9:11; Jeremiah 10:22; Jeremiah 49:33; Jeremiah 51:37; Lamentations 5:18; Ezekiel 13:4; Malachi 1:3).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: People with a comfortable life had skin protected from the sun and wind. Dark skin suggested physical and social decline (Lamentations 4:8; Lamentations 5:10).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Job made a promise with himself about his eyes, including an oath against himself (curse) (see Matthew 5:28–29). Job might have focused on wrong desire because the eyes are often the first to commit sin (Genesis 3:6). 

• Looking with wrong desire at a virgin violates the spirit of the seventh commandment (Deuteronomy 5:18, see Matthew 5:27–28). It could violate the tenth commandment as well (Deuteronomy 5:21).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job called down wrong against himself (curses) if he was guilty of the accusations against him. Apart from mentioning idolatry (worship of false gods), Job spoke about how loyal he was to God by focusing on the second half of the Ten Commandments (Job 31:26–27). The summary of these is: “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18; Romans 13:9).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• If Job had lied in a business deal, it would violate the eighth commandment (Deuteronomy 5:19). If he lied in court, it would violate the ninth commandment (Deuteronomy 5:20). This sin would deserve judgment of fire (Revelation 21:8).

• If Job desired his neighbor's possessions, he would violate the tenth commandment (Deuteronomy 5:21).

• then may another eat: This was also speaking against himself (a curse).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Whether she tempted him or he waited for her, if Job desired his neighbor’s wife, he would violate the seventh and tenth commandments (Job 24:15–16; Deuteronomy 5:18, Matthew 5:27–28; Deuteronomy 5:21).

• grind for: This might refer to servitude or sexual relations (Exodus 11:5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The Hebrew term zimmah is associated with sexual crimes like incest (“it is depraved,” Leviticus 18:17), gang-rape (“a lewd and disgraceful act,” Judges 20:6), and prostitution ("indecency," Ezekiel 23:49).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The Old Testament rarely links fire with hell (Abaddon) or the grave (see Deuteronomy 32:22).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Rejected … manservant or maidservant: This might refer to violating the fourth commandment (Deuteronomy 5:12–15).

• He who made me in the womb also make them: Job applied the idea of being made in God's image to the poor person and even to slaves (Proverbs 14:31; Proverbs 22:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: I had support in the gate: Job had respect and they regarded him as part of the high class (Job 29:7–10).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: If someone used an arm for a sinful action, having it torn from its socket would be a fitting punishment (Job 31:21). This would be better than encountering God's judgment (compare Matthew 5:28–30).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: If I have put my trust in gold: Job did not state the result of this vow because the "if-then" pattern was now obvious (Job 31:5–23). He rejected the judgment Eliphaz implied (Job 22:24–25; see Psalms 52:7; Psalms 62:10; 1 Timothy 6:10, 1 Timothy 6:17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: rejoiced in my great wealth: See Deuteronomy 8:17–18; compare Isaiah 10:12–14; Daniel 4:28–30; Hosea 12:8.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: if I have beheld the sun … or the moon: This vow denies violating the first commandment (compare Jeremiah 8:2; Jeremiah 44:17; Ezekiel 8:16; Acts 7:43; Deuteronomy 5:7; see Deuteronomy 4:19; Deuteronomy 17:2–7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The sins of adultery and worshiping the sun and moon had the death penalty (compare Job 31:1, Job 31:9–12). Both were sins that tempted the inner being of a person through the eyes. Judges tried both types of sin in court.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• My heart was secretly enticed: See Job 31:9. 

• threw a kiss from my mouth: Compare 1 Kings 19:18; Hosea 13:2.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• In Israel, the role of judges was to punish those worshiping idols (false gods) by execution (see Job 31:11; Deuteronomy 17:2–7). 

• Denying God on high violated the first commandment (Deuteronomy 5:7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• I have rejoiced in my enemy’s ruin: See Proverbs 24:17–18; compare 2 Samuel 16:5–8.

• Speaking evil against (a curse) anyone went against the spirit of the sixth commandment (Deuteronomy 5:17; see Matthew 5:21–22).

• It was against God's will to seek revenge (Matthew 5:43–44; Romans 12:14; James 3:6–10; 1 Peter 3:9).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: no stranger had to lodge on the street: The Old Testament values hosting strangers (hospitality) (Genesis 18:1–13; Genesis 19:2–3; Judges 19:20–21). The New Testament commands it (Matthew 25:35; Romans 12:13; 1 Timothy 3:2; Hebrews 13:2; 1 Peter 4:9).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Here is my signature: Job wanted to make the events official (Job 19:23–24).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: carry it on my shoulder (compare Exodus 28:12; Isaiah 22:22): He would take full responsibility for his actions.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: When someone made a wrong accusation against a prince, he could appeal to his king.

entries.title: Job
