entries.content: The land was the main "witness" to the crimes done on it (Job 20:27; see Genesis 4:10; compare James 5:4).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: let briers grow: Job cursed himself (spoke evil against himself), echoing when God first "cursed" Adam (Genesis 3:17–18; see also Isaiah 7:25; Zephaniah 2:9).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's three friends did not succeed in comforting him (see Job 2:11; Job 6:14–30; Job 13:4; Job 16:2; Job 19:21; Job 42:10).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: After three rounds of speeches between Job and his friends, a new voice speaks. Elihu, a young man, has listened to everything the others said.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The Buzite: Buz had ties with Aram and Arabia, similar to Uz (Genesis 22:21; Jeremiah 25:23; Job 1:1).

• Elihu often said he was angry. He probably considered his anger as righteous "zeal" (Psalm 69:9).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Elihu respected elders, following a common principle (see also Job 12:12; Job 15:10; Leviticus 19:32; 1 Timothy 5:1; 1 Peter 5:5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The spirit in a man might not be God's Spirit of prophecy that Elihu later mentions, as Eliphaz had done (Job 33:14–15; Job 4:12–17; compare Job 32:18–20). This spirit might simply exist because of creation (Job 33:4; Genesis 2:7; Acts 17:25).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Some translations read, "you are silent, now that you stand and no longer reply." Thus, Elihu addresses Job's friends. The Berean Standard Bible translates they are silent, now that they stand and no longer reply. This interprets Elihu talking to Job about his friends.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The length of Elihu’s speech shows he had many words to share (Job 32:1–37:24).

• Elihu probably believed the spirit (Hebrew ruakh) within him urged him to speak (Job 32:8, Job 32:19–20; Psalm 39:3). But the reader might regard him as just full of wind (an alternate meaning of the Hebrew ruakh; see study note on Job 15:2–3).

• Like Zophar, Elihu needed to speak to find relief (compare Job 20:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: hear: Elihu asked the others to hear him, just as Job had also requested (Job 33:1; Job 34:2, Job 34:16; Job 13:6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Elihu invited Job to present his case, acting as if he were God or the judge Job had been seeking (Job 9:32–35).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• no fear of me should terrify you: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar had tried to use God's terrors to scare Job (Job 15:21, Job 15:24; Job 22:10; Job 18:11, Job 18:14; Job 20:25; Job 6:4; Job 7:14; Job 9:34; Job 13:21; Job 23:15).

• Elihu promised not to be harsh with Job, but he later violated his promise (Job 34:7–9, Job 34:33–37).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job claimed to be pure and without sin, using various terms (Job 9:21; Job 10:6–7; Job 11:4; Job 13:23–24; Job 15:14–16; Job 16:17; Job 31:1–40).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job often complained about God's constant surveillance (Job 7:20; Job 10:14; Job 13:27). He wanted relief from having every move examined (Job 14:16; Job 29:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's main complaint was that God did not answer him (Job 9:16; Job 19:7; Job 23:2–7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: In a dream: For examples, see Genesis 15:12; Genesis 20:3; Genesis 31:24; Genesis 40:1–41:36; Daniel 2:1–45; Joel 2:28; Acts 16:9–10.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: from perishing by the sword: This phrase can also mean "from crossing over the river of death" (New Living Translation). Both translations make sense in the context (compare Job 36:12).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: messengers of death: Compare: Exodus 12:23; 2 Samuel 24:16; 1 Corinthians 10:10.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: An angel or messenger from heaven would act as the mediator Job desired (see Job 5:1; Job 9:33–34; Job 16:18–21).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The ultimate ransom is Christ (Matthew 20:28; Romans 3:24–25; 1 Timothy 2:6; 1 Peter 1:18–19).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: he sees God’s face and shouts for joy: Compare Numbers 6:24–26; Psalm 67:1; Acts 2:28; Jude 1:24.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: It sounds ironic that Elihu says he would like to vindicate Job. He joined the discussion because Job would not admit he had sinned (Job 32:1–5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: ear tests … mouth tastes: Elihu repeated Job’s earlier complaint about the other counselors’ weak argument that, "Wisdom is found with the elderly" (Job 12:11–12; see Job 6:30; Hebrews 5:14).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job said he was righteous: See Job 9:20–21; Job 13:18; Job 27:6.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Eliphaz accused Job of lying (Job 15:5). This was something Job feared would happen (Job 6:28–29).

• My wound (literally My arrow): For the connection with the Lord’s "arrows," see Job 6:4; Job 16:13; Jeremiah 10:19; Jeremiah 15:18; Jeremiah 30:12, Jeremiah 30:15; Lamentations 3:12; Micah 1:9; Nahum 3:19.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Elihu later repeated this accusation (Job 35:3; compare Psalm 73:13; Zephaniah 1:12; Malachi 3:14). But he misrepresented Job’s words (Job 9:22–23; Job 21:15). Job had actually criticized those who had this perspective (Job 21:14–16).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
The passage connects three ideas to the belief that God can do no wrong (Job 34:10, Job 34:12): 

• God rewards or punishes people based on their actions (Job 34:11); 

• As the creator, God does not have to answer to anyone (Job 34:13). 

• Every living being relies on God for life. God can take life away without being wrong (Job 34:14–15; compare Romans 9:19–29).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: according to a man’s deeds: Compare Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12; Jeremiah 32:19; Ezekiel 33:20; Matthew 16:27; Romans 2:6; Galatians 6:7–8; 1 Peter 1:17. The final judgment will occur at the end of time (2 Corinthians 5:10; Revelation 2:23; Revelation 22:12).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The implication was that God could not rule if he hated justice (see Romans 3:4–7; Romans 7:7, Romans 7:13; Romans 9:14; Galatians 2:17; Galatians 6:14).

• Later, God also asked if Job intended to condemn the mighty judge (Job 40:8).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: who is not partial to princes: God's justice is not partial (Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11; Galatians 2:6; Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 3:25; 1 Peter 1:17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Evil people may try to hide in darkness (Jeremiah 23:24). But they will not succeed (Psalm 139:11–12; compare Amos 9:2–3). God reveals everything (1 Corinthians 4:5).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: God need not examine a man further: Elihu said this to disagree with Job's wish for God to quickly announce a time of judgment (Job 21:19; Job 24:1). Elihu believed that God already understood all people perfectly without needing to set up a special court or investigation.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• God knows everything without needing to ask anyone (Job 34:25).

• sets up others in their place: Daniel 2:21; Daniel 5:28–30.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: When God shows justice openly, it causes evil people to have proper fear (Deuteronomy 21:21; 1 Timothy 5:20). This leads to public joy among people in a right relationship with God (compare Exodus 14:30–31).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Suppose someone says: Elihu posed the indirect question, "Job, why won't you admit it?"

entries.title: Job
entries.content: tried to the utmost: Zophar also said that Job should have suffered worse punishment than he did (Job 11:6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
Elihu tried to answer his own question (Job 35:2). 

But his response did not add anything new compared to:

• Zophar (Job 11:8–9).

• Eliphaz (Job 22:12).

• Bildad (Job 25:5–6).

• Job (Job 9:8–10). 

Elihu did not realize that all sin offends God (Genesis 39:9; Matthew 25:41–46; compare Proverbs 19:17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Elihu echoed Job's words but then disagreed with them (Job 9:24; Job 12:6–10; Job 21:7–15, Job 21:17).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Elihu echoed his earlier accusation (Job 34:35). Later, God would agree (Job 38:2).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: one who is perfect in knowledge is with you: Elihu probably was claiming to be sincere or that his logic had no flaw.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The Bible teaches that God always watches over the righteous (2 Chronicles 16:9; Psalms 33:18; Psalms 34:15; 1 Peter 3:12). This idea addresses Job's frustration about God's surveillance (Job 7:17–21).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: If they obey and serve Him, then they end their days in prosperity: This is a true biblical principle of dedication to God (repentance) (see Job 11:13–19; Job 22:21–25; Deuteronomy 4:30; Jeremiah 7:23; Jeremiah 26:13).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: die without knowledge: See also Job 4:21; Proverbs 5:23; Proverbs 10:21.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The Hebrew yadin typically means he judges or he governs. But some commentators propose an alternate reading, yazun (meaning "he nourishes"). This aligns with the theme of God's provision (Job 38:26; Psalms 65:9–13; Psalms 104:13–15, Psalms 104:27–28). The more common meaning of yadin is “judge,” which would mean that God does all things to bless his people and judge his enemies (Job 37:11–13; Job 38:22–23; see Genesis 6:17; Genesis 19:24; Exodus 9:23–25; Joshua 10:11–14; 1 Samuel 12:18).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The Old Testament often links thunder to God's voice (Job 36:29, Job 36:33; Job 37:5; Job 38:1; Exodus 19:16–19; Psalm 104:7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: He seals up the hand of every man … know His work: The end of the farming season gives people time to think about God's control over everything.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: God's actions can have multiple purposes. For example, storms can both destroy enemies and bring victory to God's people (Joshua 10; Judges 4; 1 Samuel 7:10–11; Psalms 18:7–15; Psalms 105:32–33).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The hot south wind made it very hot and uncomfortable.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Should He be told that I want to speak? Would a man ask to be swallowed up?: Contesting God's judgment might lead to severe punishment, even death (see Job 13:14).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Out of the north (Hebrew from Zaphon): In the literature of the ancient city of Ugarit, Zaphon was the northern mountain home of the false god "Baal." Here, it symbolically refers to the height of God's home in the heavens (see Isaiah 14:13–14).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The Almighty is beyond our reach: Compare Job 11:7; Job 26:14; Romans 11:33; 1 Timothy 6:16.

• His justice and great righteousness: Compare Job 9:4, Job 9:19; Job 12:13; Psalms 62:11; Psalms 66:3; Psalms 93:1; Psalms 99:4.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind: The Old Testament often links storms with God's presence (2 Kings 2:1, 2 Kings 2:11; Ezekiel 1:4; Nahum 1:3). Job finally had the chance to speak with God (Job 13:22–23).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: God challenges Job. Job admits he cannot judge the moral world. God shows Job's ignorance of the natural world's elements related to the realm of heaven, weather, animals, and birds (Job 38:4–21; Job 38:22–38; Job 38:39–39:30).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Then the LORD answered Job: In this last part, the LORD challenges Job's strong self-defense by showing his works. This reminds Job of God's supreme greatness.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: obscures My counsel: God’s accusation is similar to a charge made by Eliphaz and Elihu (Job 15:2; Job 34:35; Job 35:16). Job eventually admitted his guilt (Job 42:3).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: God describes the morning stars as if they are people, similar to the description of angels (Job 1:6; Job 2:1).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: set in place its bars and doors: God describes the sea as a dangerous creature that is kept under control.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: stand out like the folds of a garment: The rising sun highlights the colors, shapes, and textures of objects.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: you were already born: Compare with Proverbs 8:25. This sarcasm is similar to Eliphaz's words in Job 15:7.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: God stores up snow and hail, like the deep seas and winds (Psalms 33:7; Psalms 135:7; Jeremiah 10:13; Jeremiah 51:16). God uses these elements as weapons through storms he sends on the day of war and battle (Job 36:32; Isaiah 30:30; Ezekiel 13:11–13; Revelation 16:21; for example, Joshua 10:11; Judges 5:20–21; 1 Samuel 7:10.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The east wind blows from the desert, drying up crops and seas (Genesis 41:6, Genesis 41:23, Genesis 41:27; Jeremiah 4:11; Jonah 4:8; Exodus 14:21; Isaiah 11:15). It is not like the heavy rain that causes floods.

• Helpful rain quenches a barren land (Psalms 104:10–11; Psalms 107:35; Isaiah 35:7; Isaiah 58:11). This contrasts with both hot winds and flooding rains (Job 38:24, 25).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: heart … mind: These words can also mean "ibis" and "rooster." The Egyptians believed the ibis bird knew about the Nile's flooding, the most important event in Egypt. Israel’s rabbis (religious teachers with authority) believed the rooster bird could predict rain or its distinctive sound (crowing) marked day and night. The question would then be Who taught the ibis and the rooster? See also Psalm 51:6; Proverbs 2:6; James 1:5, James 1:17.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: the wild donkey … scorns the tumult of the city: This is the first example in a series of animals that think little of other animals not their equal (compare Job 39:18, Job 39:22; Job 41:29). These images show how God scorns the opposition of a person like Job (see Psalm 2:4).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The wild ox now no longer exists and was already rare by the time of Moses. It was the strongest land animal in early Canaan. They never tamed this Old Testament symbol of strength (Numbers 23:22; Numbers 24:8; Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalms 29:6; Psalms 92:10; compare Genesis 1:28; Genesis 9:2; Psalm 8:5–6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: In the ancient Near East, people believed the ostrich was a bird that God had not given wisdom.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
The ostrich symbolizes neglect for her young because she (Lamentations 4:3): 

• Leaves her eggs on the ground.

• Seems to abandon her eggs when a predator comes near. She is probably trying to distract the predator from the nest.

• Lays her eggs with other female ostrich in a shared nest, so many eggs are not her own.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: laughs at the horse and its rider: See Job 39:7, Job 39:22; Job 41:29.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: They blew the ram's horn in battle to signal the attack (Joshua 6:4–6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Where there is a dead body, you will find the eagle feeding on the remains (Ezekiel 39:17–19; Matthew 24:28; Luke 17:37).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) does not include the end of God's first speech.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's short and humble reply does not admit guilt, but it does admit how "insignificant" he is (Job 40:4). Earlier, he believed he could approach God like a prince or even question him (Job 31:37; Job 13:22–23).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• I am insignificant (compare Job 42:6): Job was not asking God to forgive his sin. Like Abraham, he recognized that he was not worthy (Genesis 18:27).

• Job had asked those comforting him to cover their mouths to show shock (Job 21:5). Here, he does so himself in reaction to his own inappropriate words.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: I have nothing to add: He had no more accusations against God and would not argue again.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: The LORD repeated his earlier challenge (refer to Job 38:1–3).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's words had angered Elihu (Job 10:7; Job 27:2; Job 31:35–37; Job 32:2; Job 34:5). Now, God himself challenged Job's words.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job could not humble proud people without God's authority (Isaiah 2:11–12, Isaiah 2:17; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5–6; Malachi 4:3; Romans 16:20).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• After listing natural animals, God described Behemoth and "Leviathan" as creatures humans cannot control (Job 39:1–30; Job 40:15–24; Job 41:1–34). Job could not control the wild donkey or ox (Job 39:5–12; Job 40:15–24). However, God created and could control them, and Job had to accept this fact (Job 41:2).

• Here, Behemoth appears to be a natural creature: 

• It is an animal God made, just as he made Job (Job 40:15).

• It is not a fierce predator but eats grass like an ox (Job 40:15).

• It is in a poem about God’s creation of the natural world, not in a myth about the world's formation. Most commentators think Behemoth is the hippopotamus, a large, grass-eating animal (Job 40:15–19). It rests in the river among lotus plants and reeds (Job 40:21). Like the wild ox, Behemoth is strong (Job 40:16–18, Job 40:24; Job 39:11). Yet it is mostly peaceful (Job 40:20–23).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
Unlike the peaceful Behemoth (Job 40:15–24), Leviathan was a threat (see also Job 3:8; Psalms 74:14; Psalms 104:26; Isaiah 27:1). Most scholars think Leviathan was like a crocodile, with its powerful jaws and tough skin twisting and turning in the water (Job 41:14; Job 41:15–17, Job 41:23; Job 41:31–32). But Leviathan is a fire-breathing dragon that wraps around the sun to cause the sun to seem covered (Job 41:18–21; Job 3:8–9). 

The background for Leviathan is the seven-headed sea monster symbolizing chaos in ancient Near Eastern mythology. In the Bible, this wild sea creature often represents chaos and evil, whose head the Lord crushes (Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1; compare Job 9:13; Job 26:12; Psalm 89:9–10; Isaiah 30:7; Isaiah 51:9). Later in the Bible, Satan is linked to the ancient serpent and great dragon (Genesis 3; Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2). Christ and his followers crush his head (Romans 16:20).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job understood the message of God’s speeches: I know that You can do all things. Nothing is too hard for him (Genesis 18:14; Jeremiah 32:17; Matthew 19:26). Job says, No plan of Yours can be thwarted (Job 23:13; Isaiah 14:27; Isaiah 46:10). Job realized how different he was from God.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: now my eyes have seen You: Before this, Job had not seen God (see Job 23:8). Now, like the prophet Isaiah, he has been in God's presence and feels overwhelmed by how holy God is (Isaiah 6:1).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Eliphaz the Temanite was the spokesperson for the friends, probably because of he was older. Eliphaz had a false claim that his advice came from visions of prophecy (Job 4:12–16). Now God spoke to him, but not to support his message.

• Unlike his three friends, Job spoke accurately about God (compare Job 13:7–10). Job’s direct questions were more effective in finding out the truth about God than the friends’ shallow definitions of doctrine.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The LORD made Job the "mediator" that Job had hoped to find for himself and that Elihu wanted to be (Job 9:33; Job 16:19–21; Job 19:25; Job 32:1–37:24).

• go to My servant Job: God wanted Job’s friends to make peace with Job before they offered their gifts (Matthew 5:23–24).

• My servant Job will pray for you: He had also prayed for his children (Job 1:5; compare James 5:16; 1 John 5:16).

• When the LORD accepted Job’s prayer, it ironically fulfilled Eliphaz’s promise (Job 22:26–30).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: Job's fortunes probably included his health (Job 42:16–17). God created humans to bless them, not to do them harm (curse).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Even though God restored Job, he still needed comfort for the loss of his children. His family and former friends continued to support him, following Job's earlier practices, taking over where the three friends had stopped (Job 4:4; Job 16:5; Job 2:11; compare 2 Corinthians 7:6).

• The money given to Job was not just charity to increase his wealth again. It was also to honor him and gain favor from an influential man (for example, Proverbs 18:16). It might also have been to ease any lack of favor (for example, Genesis 32:20; Genesis 33:10; Genesis 43:11; 1 Samuel 25:27).

• Women wore a gold ring in their nose (Genesis 24:47; Proverbs 11:22; Isaiah 3:21). Both men and women wore them on the ears (Genesis 35:4; Exodus 32:2–3; Judges 8:24).

entries.title: Job
entries.content: When God blessed Job, it ironically fulfilled Bildad’s promise (Job 8:7).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The names of Job’s new daughters reflect his good fortune God had renewed: 

• Jemimah means “dove” (see Song 2:14). 

• Keziah means “cassia” or “cinnamon flower” (see Psalm 45:8). 

• Keren-happuch means “horn of antimony,” which is a shiny container for make-up.

entries.title: Job
entries.content: their father granted them an inheritance among their brothers: Daughters usually inherited only if there were no male children (Numbers 27; Numbers 36:36). Perhaps Job's unusual action indicated his great wealth. Only a rich man could give some wealth to the families into which his daughters would marry.

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• Job lived for 140 more years, which was about twice as long as a normal life (Psalm 90:10). If God gave him double what he had before (Job 42:10), Job may have already been 70 years old, making his total life 210 years. This would fit the time of the early patriarchs in the Bible (see Genesis 25:7; Genesis 35:28; Genesis 47:28; Genesis 50:26; Deuteronomy 34:7; Joshua 24:29). 

• to the fourth generation: God blessed Job by letting him live long enough to see his children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and great-great-grandchildren grow up (Genesis 50:23; Psalm 128:6).

entries.title: Job
entries.content:
• The patriarchs ("first fathers") Abraham and Isaac also died at an old age (Genesis 25:8; Genesis 35:29). Job too lived a long, full life. This fulfilled Eliphaz’s promise (Job 5:26). His promise had its basis on God's general promise (Deuteronomy 6:2; Psalm 91:16).

• At the end of the book, the ancient Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) adds a note saying that Job will resurrect from the dead at the final resurrection. It also provides information about where and when Job and those who descended from him lived.
